title: Read a Finished Building Backwards
summary: A finished building is a record of hundreds of decisions about structure, systems, sequence and cost. Ford and Marco teach a method for reading that record from the outside in, so you can copy what worked and avoid what the builder paid for in silence.
body:
A finished building is the answer to a set of questions you can no longer hear; reverse engineering means reconstructing the questions, the structure, the systems, the sequence and the cost, so that you copy the reasoning rather than the result.

Recall

Q. What is the difference between substantial completion and final completion?

A. Substantial completion is the point at which the owner can occupy and use the work for its intended purpose, with a punch list of minor items still open. Final completion is when every item, document and obligation is closed and the last payment, including retainage, is due.

Q. What is a time bar in a construction contract?

A. A clause that makes giving notice of a claim within a stated period a condition of the claim, so that late notice can extinguish an otherwise valid entitlement. Whether a court enforces it strictly depends on the wording and the governing law.

Q. Why does the water-cement ratio matter in a concrete mix?

A. Because more water relative to cement makes concrete easier to place but weaker and more permeable once it cures. The ratio is the main lever on strength and durability, which is why adding water on site is controlled.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Marco joins me this week because this subject sits between our two seats. I study what went wrong. Marco runs projects so that it does not. A finished building is where both views meet. Every completed tower in your market is a free lesson that somebody else paid for: in design fees, in delays, in rework that never appears in the brochure. Most developers walk past those lessons. They admire the lobby and ask the price per unit. You are going to learn to read the building the way an investigator reads a site, from evidence, and to come away with decisions you can use.

The four questions

Plain English first. When you stand in front of a finished building, ask four questions in order. How does it stand up? How does it breathe and serve its occupants? In what order was it built? And what did it cost per unit of useful space? Structure, systems, sequence and cost. Each answer constrains the next. The structure decides how fast the floors could go up. The systems decide how much space was given away to shafts and plant rooms. The sequence decides how long the money was out. The cost is the sum of all three.

The professional framing is that a building is a set of trade-offs that were locked in early. The structural grid, the column spacing, decided the parking layout, the unit widths and the formwork. The core position decided the elevator count and the corridor length. The floor-to-floor height, the distance from one floor surface to the next, decided the facade area and therefore a large share of the envelope cost. When you reverse engineer, you are trying to find the two or three early decisions that drove everything else.

Reading structure and systems from outside

You can learn a great deal without a single drawing. Count the floors and measure the height to estimate floor-to-floor. Look at the facade for a repeating rhythm: column lines often show as a regular bay. Look for a change in that rhythm part way up, which may mean a transfer level, a heavy floor that moves column loads sideways because the columns above do not line up with those below. Transfer floors are expensive and slow, so a building that avoids one has usually made a good early decision.

Worked example one, hypothetical. You visit a 20-floor residential tower. From the street you count 20 floors over a tall ground floor and estimate the total height at about 64 metres. Take off roughly 5 metres for the ground floor and roof structure. That leaves about 59 metres for 19 typical floors, or a floor-to-floor of about 3.1 metres. Inside, you see flat slabs with no beams and a bulkhead only over the corridor. That tells you the designer chose a thin post-tensioned or flat plate slab, kept ductwork in the corridor, and bought back facade area by keeping the floor-to-floor tight. Each 0.1 metre saved on 19 floors is almost 2 metres of facade and structure that was never built.

Systems leave traces too. Rooftop units, louvres on every floor, or a mechanical floor tell you how the building is cooled and ventilated. A cluster of louvres on each balcony suggests individual units in each apartment. A single plant room suggests a central system. Each choice moves capital cost, operating cost and the floor area given to shafts.

Say that out loud now.

Structure, systems, sequence, cost. Find the two or three early decisions that drove the rest.

Reading sequence and cost

Sequence is the order of construction, and it is where the money goes. In a concrete tower, the core, the stair and elevator walls, usually rises first and leads the floor slabs by a few levels. The slabs follow on a repeating floor cycle, the number of working days to form, reinforce, pour and strip one typical floor. The envelope follows the slabs several floors behind, and interior trades follow the envelope once floors are dry. The finished building tells you whether this flowed: identical typical floors, a repeating facade panel and stacked bathrooms are signs that the design was made for repetition, which is what makes a short cycle possible.

Worked example two, hypothetical. Public records show a building permit issued in month 0 and an occupancy certificate in month 26. You estimate 4 months for foundations and below-grade work, 6 months for the final fit-out and commissioning after the structure tops out, and the rest for structure with overlapping envelope. That leaves 16 months, about 350 working days, for the superstructure of 20 floors plus podium. Even allowing 60 working days for the podium, that implies a typical floor cycle of around 14 working days. That is slow for a repetitive tower. Now you have a question to ask the builder: was the cycle slow by design, because of a single crane, or slow by trouble, because of approvals, labour or concrete supply?

Cost comes last because it is the least reliable number you will hear. A quoted cost per square metre means nothing until you know the area basis, the scope included, the date and the location. Quincy will take that apart on Day 3.

How the best do it

The contractors who build the world's tallest towers treat the typical floor as a manufacturing line. They decide the floor cycle during design, not after award, and then size the system to it: a self-climbing formwork system for the core, a table or panel formwork system for slabs that is lifted rather than rebuilt, reinforcement assembled into cages at ground level, concrete pumped to height from a mix designed to gain strength fast enough for the cycle, and a crane and hoist plan that is checked hour by hour against the cycle. They plan the work in zones, so each trade moves through the floor in a fixed rhythm. A small developer can copy the logic without the equipment: design for repetition, set a realistic cycle with the structural engineer and the contractor before pricing, and make the logistics plan prove the cycle. What to avoid is copying the cycle time itself. The cycle is an output of a system; borrow the number without the system and you have borrowed a promise you cannot keep.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: what you learn from a benchmark does not change how costs are capitalised or deducted, but a benchmark study bought from a consultant is a soft cost whose treatment you should confirm; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: drawings and data from another owner are usually protected, so learn from what you may lawfully see. Banking: lenders and their monitors respect a schedule that cites real comparable buildings. Governance: record each benchmark, its source and what you decided because of it. Estate: a library of benchmarks and lessons is part of the know-how that outlives any one project. Exit: buyers pay for efficient floor plates and durable systems, which is exactly what reverse engineering teaches you to recognise.

Professional sign-off required: structural engineer, on any structural conclusion drawn from observation; cost consultant, on any benchmark cost used in a budget.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is copying an outcome without its conditions: adopting another building's cost or cycle time while your site, crane, labour market, design and concrete supply are different. The control is to write beside every benchmark number the conditions that produced it, and to refuse to use the number until each condition is matched or adjusted.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner tours a finished building, admires the finishes and leaves with a price per unit. The professional leaves with a floor-to-floor height, a grid, a core position, a cycle estimate and three questions for the builder.

Callback

In Week 17, Sage taught you to reverse engineer a deal from public information: to work back from a sale price and a rent to an implied land value and return. This week applies the same discipline to the physical building. The method is the same in both. Start from what is visible and certain, state each assumption you add, and treat the answer as a range that improves with every confirmed fact.

Recap

Read a finished building in four passes: structure, systems, sequence and cost. Find the early decisions, the grid, the core, the floor-to-floor and the degree of repetition, that drove everything else. Treat every benchmark number as the output of a system, and copy the system before you copy the number.

Next: Ford on Failure Forensics: a composite case of a borrowed floor cycle that the site could not deliver.
checklist: I read every benchmark building in four passes: structure, systems, sequence and cost.
I estimate floor-to-floor height and look for transfer levels before I discuss price.
I note the core position, the grid and how much of the design repeats.
I check public permit and occupancy dates to estimate the real construction duration.
I write the conditions beside every benchmark number: site, crane, formwork, labour and date.
I take questions to the builder, not conclusions.
I record each benchmark and the decision it informed in my project file.
I get a structural engineer and a cost consultant to review any conclusion I rely on.
head: Field checklist
speak: A finished building is a record of decisions. Read it in four passes: how it stands up, how its systems serve it, in what order it was built, and what it cost per unit of useful space. Structure, systems, sequence, cost. The goal is to find the two or three early decisions that drove everything else: the column grid, the core position, the floor-to-floor height and how much of the design repeats. From the street you can estimate floor-to-floor by dividing height by floors, and look for a transfer level where the facade rhythm changes. From public permit and occupancy dates you can estimate how long the structure took and the floor cycle it implies. The best tall-building contractors design the floor cycle first and size cranes, formwork and concrete to it. Copy that logic, never the cycle time itself, because a borrowed number without its system is a promise you cannot keep.
terms: Floor-to-floor height — the vertical distance from the surface of one floor to the surface of the next, which drives facade, structure and services cost.
Transfer floor — a heavy structural level that carries column loads sideways because the columns above do not line up with those below.
Floor cycle — the number of working days needed to form, reinforce, pour and strip one typical floor of a building.

hostile.q: You keep citing that tower down the street as proof your schedule works. Did you build it, or do you just like it?
hostile.a: I did not build it, and I am not relying on liking it. I used it for three facts I could verify: the permit and occupancy dates, the floor-to-floor height and the degree of repetition. From those I estimated its structural duration and floor cycle as a range, and I wrote down the conditions that produced it: one crane, handset formwork and a conventional mix. Our schedule matches or adjusts each condition, and our structural engineer and contractor have reviewed it. If any condition differs, I can show you where the schedule carries the difference.

title: The Borrowed Floor Cycle: A Composite
summary: A composite case: a developer adopted a celebrated tower's floor cycle without its cranes, formwork or concrete, fell behind, and recovered time by stripping formwork on the calendar instead of on measured strength. A slab cracked, and the recovery cost more than the delay it was meant to save.
body:
This is a composite example. A developer borrowed a fast floor cycle from a famous building, could not deliver it, and recovered the schedule by stripping formwork early; the slab that cracked cost more time and money than the delay ever would have.

Recall

Q. What is a punch list?

A. The list of minor incomplete or defective items recorded at substantial completion, which the contractor must close before final completion and the release of the last payment.

Q. What is concurrent delay?

A. Delay to completion caused at the same time by both an owner event and a contractor event. How it is treated, for time and for money, depends on the contract wording and the governing law.

Q. What does a concrete cylinder test measure?

A. The compressive strength of samples taken from the pour and cured under controlled conditions, tested at set ages to show whether the delivered concrete meets the specified strength.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, yesterday we learned to read a finished building. Today we watch what happens when someone reads one badly. Nobody in this story was reckless. Everyone was trying to save time. That is the most common shape of a construction failure, and it is the reason I want the rule at the end written on the inside of your site diary. This is a composite example, assembled from patterns that recur in concrete construction. The numbers are hypothetical round figures.

1. Timeline

A developer plans a hypothetical 30-floor concrete residential tower. In month 1, he adopts a 4-day typical floor cycle, citing a celebrated tower in another city. In month 4, the contract is signed on that schedule with liquidated damages, a fixed daily amount owed for late completion. In month 9, the typical floors begin. The real cycle runs 7 days from the start. By month 12 the job is 6 weeks behind. In month 13, to recover, the site team strips slab formwork and removes the shores, the temporary supports under a fresh slab, at 3 days whatever the concrete has achieved. In month 14, a slab two floors below the active deck shows wide cracks and visible sag. The structural engineer stops work on the tower, orders full reshoring and core tests, and in month 15 part of one slab is cut out and recast. The job finishes 5 months late.

2. Key decisions

Three decisions mattered. Adopting a cycle time as a target without checking the system behind it. Signing a contract that tied liquidated damages to that cycle. And, when it slipped, recovering time by stripping on the calendar rather than on strength, a decision made on site without the engineer of record, the engineer legally responsible for the structural design.

3. Assumptions

The developer assumed the benchmark cycle was a property of good management. It was a property of a system: a self-climbing core form, table forms lifted floor to floor, two cranes, a high-early-strength mix and a crew that had built the same floor many times. The site had one crane, handset formwork, a standard mix and a new crew. The superintendent assumed that because 3-day cylinders had passed on earlier floors they would pass again. The weather had turned cold, and cold slows strength gain.

4. Incentives

The contractor faced liquidated damages on every day of delay, so every incentive pointed at speed. The developer faced interest on a fully drawn loan and a pre-sale buyer base expecting a date. The formwork crew was paid by the floor. Nobody in the chain was paid for patience, and the one person whose job was to say "not yet", the engineer of record, had not been asked.

Say that out loud now.

Formwork comes off on strength, not on the calendar. The engineer decides what strength means.

5. Warning signs ignored

The cycle never once hit 4 days, which meant the plan was wrong from the first floor, not drifting. The crane was booked for formwork lifts, rebar and concrete buckets at the same hours. Field-cured cylinders, samples kept on the deck in the same conditions as the slab, were not being made, so the only strength data came from laboratory-cured samples kept warm. Hairline cracks appeared on two earlier floors and were logged as shrinkage. The night temperatures dropped and no one changed the stripping time.

6. Point of no return

The point of no return was the first day the slab was stripped at 3 days without a measured in-place strength. Up to then, the job could have been re-sequenced, a second crane rented, a faster mix specified or the schedule re-baselined with the lender. After that day, the job was carrying fresh slabs on concrete that had not been proven, and the only question was which floor would show it first.

Notice what the developer could still have chosen at month 12. He could have asked the contractor for a recovery schedule with named resources, the subject of Week 118. He could have bought time with equipment rather than with risk. He could have opened a conversation with the lender about a revised completion date. Each option cost money. None of them cost a slab.

7. Root cause

The root cause was not the cold weather or the crew. It was a schedule copied from an outcome without its system, and then a stripping decision based on time rather than on evidence. The first error created the pressure; the second converted pressure into a structural defect. Concrete codes and formwork guidance in the United States, including the American Concrete Institute's documents, place formwork removal and reshoring under the control of strength criteria and the responsible engineer; verify the exact requirements against the current adopted edition.

What it cost

Worked example, hypothetical. The original delay was 6 weeks. Recovery by early stripping produced a 5-month delay instead. At a hypothetical carry of 200,000 dollars a month for interest and site overheads, the 5 months cost 1,000,000 dollars, against 300,000 dollars for the original 6 weeks. Add 400,000 dollars to remove and recast the slab, 150,000 dollars for testing and engineering, and liquidated damages exposure the parties then fought over. A second crane for 4 months might have cost 200,000 dollars. The cheapest option was the one nobody priced.

A second calculation, hypothetical, shows the system mismatch. The benchmark cycle of 4 days on 30 floors gives 120 working days of typical floors. The site's real cycle of 7 days gives 210. That 90-day gap existed on the day the contract was signed. It was not lost on site; it was promised away at the desk.

Professional sign-off required: structural engineer of record, on formwork stripping and reshoring criteria; formwork engineer, on the shoring design.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a recovery decision taken on site, under pressure, that trades a schedule problem for a structural one. The control is a written stripping and reshoring procedure, approved by the engineer of record, that uses measured in-place strength and that nobody on site may shorten.

The beginner's mistake

Treating a famous building's cycle time as a benchmark of effort rather than of equipment. A beginner hears "4 days" and asks why his contractor is slow. A professional asks which crane, which formwork and which mix.

Callback

In Week 113, Duke taught the pre-pour checklist, curing and reshoring as field disciplines. In Week 50, Petra taught that float belongs to someone and that a schedule is a logic network, not a list of dates. This case joins the two: the schedule logic was wrong from the start, and the field discipline was the place where that error was paid for.

Recap

A developer borrowed a 4-day cycle without its cranes, formwork, mix or crew, signed liquidated damages against it, fell behind and stripped on the calendar. A slab cracked, and 6 weeks of delay became 5 months. Rule 120 follows.

Rule 120: Never adopt a benchmark cycle time until its crane, formwork, labour, concrete and inspection system is matched, and never strip or reshore on the calendar; strip only on in-place strength the engineer of record has approved.

Next: Quincy on The Money: what a cost per square metre really contains.
checklist: I write down the crane, formwork, mix and crew behind any cycle time I adopt.
I test a proposed floor cycle against the crane hook-time plan before I sign the contract.
I require a written stripping and reshoring procedure approved by the engineer of record.
I require field-cured cylinders or another in-place strength measure before stripping.
I treat a cycle that never meets plan on the first floors as a planning error, not a drift.
I price equipment and re-sequencing before I accept any recovery that touches the structure.
I tell the lender about a schedule problem early, with a recovery plan.
I log cracking on fresh slabs and send it to the engineer the same day.
head: Field checklist
speak: This is a composite case. A developer adopted a 4-day floor cycle from a famous tower for a 30-floor concrete building, and tied liquidated damages to it. The famous cycle came from two cranes, climbing and table formwork, a fast-gaining mix and an experienced crew. His site had one crane, handset forms, a standard mix and a new crew, so the cycle ran 7 days from the first floor. Six weeks behind, the site stripped formwork at 3 days regardless of strength, in cold weather, without the engineer of record. A slab cracked and sagged, part of it was recast, and 6 weeks became 5 months. The root cause was a schedule copied from an outcome without its system, and stripping on the calendar rather than on evidence. Rule 120: never adopt a benchmark cycle until its system is matched, and strip only on in-place strength the engineer has approved.
terms: Shores — temporary vertical supports that carry a fresh slab and the loads above it until the concrete is strong enough to carry itself.
Field-cured cylinders — concrete samples kept on site in the same conditions as the structure, used to estimate the strength the slab has actually reached.
Engineer of record — the licensed engineer legally responsible for the structural design and for decisions that affect it.

hostile.q: You are five months late and you say the contractor stripped too early. You signed a four-day cycle. Whose fault is the schedule?
hostile.a: Mine first. The four-day cycle was my target, and I did not check that the crane, formwork, mix and crew could deliver it before I tied damages to it. The early stripping was a site decision taken without the engineer of record, and that is a contract matter we are resolving in writing. What I can show you today is a re-baselined schedule built from our real cycle, the engineer's approved stripping procedure, and the cost to complete including the recast slab. From here every recovery option we use is priced and none of them touches the structure.

rule: Rule 120: Never adopt a benchmark cycle time until its crane, formwork, labour, concrete and inspection system is matched, and never strip or reshore on the calendar; strip only on in-place strength the engineer of record has approved.

title: What a Cost per Square Metre Really Contains
summary: A benchmark cost per square metre is only useful once you know its area basis, scope, date, location and quality. Quincy shows how to normalise a benchmark before it enters your budget, and how floor-plate efficiency changes the number that drives value.
body:
A cost per square metre is a ratio with two hidden definitions, what counts as cost and what counts as a square metre; until you know both, the number tells you nothing and can mislead you badly.

Recall

Q. What is a time impact analysis?

A. A method that inserts a delay event into the current schedule and measures how far it moves the completion date, used to support or test a claim for more time.

Q. Why do hot-weather conditions matter when placing concrete?

A. High temperatures speed up setting and evaporation, which can cause cracking and lower long-term strength, so hot-weather concreting needs planned controls such as chilled water, timing and early curing.

Q. Ford's Rule 120 says to strip formwork on what?

A. On in-place strength that the engineer of record has approved, never on the calendar.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the single most repeated number in development conversations is cost per square metre, and the single most abused. A broker says a recent tower cost 2,500 dollars a square metre. A contractor says he can build yours for 2,200. Neither number is wrong, and neither is comparable to the other until you have normalised them. Your hard cost is usually the largest line in your budget. A 10 percent error in it can erase a development spread on its own.

The two hidden definitions

Plain English first. The top of the ratio is cost. Ask what is in it. Hard costs only, the building itself? Or also site works, demolition, utility connections, parking structure, furniture, design fees, financing and land? The bottom of the ratio is area. Ask which area. Gross floor area (GFA) measures everything inside the outer walls on every floor, including corridors, shafts and plant rooms. Net saleable or net rentable area (NSA or NRA) counts only what a buyer or tenant pays for. A tower can have the same cost and two very different ratios depending on which area you divide by.

The professional framing is that a benchmark has five dimensions, and each must be matched or adjusted: area basis, scope, date, location and quality. Cost consultants use published indices to move a cost from one date to another and location factors to move it from one market to another. Those indices are commercial tools, not standards, and they differ between publishers.

Normalising a benchmark

Worked example one, hypothetical. A broker reports that a finished residential tower cost 2,400 dollars per square metre. You ask four questions and learn: it was hard cost only, measured on GFA, priced at contract award three years ago, in a city where construction is about 10 percent more expensive than yours, with a higher finish standard than you plan.

Step 1, date. A cost index shows construction prices rose a total of 15 percent over the three years. 2,400 dollars times 1.15 gives 2,760 dollars per square metre today.

Step 2, location. Their market is about 10 percent dearer. 2,760 dollars divided by 1.10 gives about 2,509 dollars per square metre in your market.

Step 3, quality. Your cost consultant estimates their finish package at about 150 dollars per square metre above yours. 2,509 dollars less 150 gives about 2,359 dollars per square metre.

Step 4, scope. Their figure excluded site works and utility connections, which on your site your consultant estimates at about 120 dollars per square metre of GFA. Add it back: about 2,479 dollars per square metre on a comparable scope.

The headline number was 2,400. The comparable number is about 2,480, and it carries four assumptions you have now written down. If the contractor offers 2,200 on your project, you now know to ask what he left out.

Say that out loud now.

Cost per square metre has two hidden definitions: what counts as cost, and which square metre.

How efficiency changes the number that drives value

Buyers and tenants pay for net area. You pay to build gross area. The ratio of net to gross is called efficiency, and it is where reverse engineering a finished building pays off, because efficient floor plates are visible: a compact core, short corridors and few shafts.

Worked example two, hypothetical. Two designs each have 10,000 square metres of GFA and a hard cost of 2,500 dollars per square metre of GFA, so 25,000,000 dollars each. Design A is 80 percent efficient, giving 8,000 square metres of net saleable area. Design B is 72 percent efficient, giving 7,200. Cost per net square metre is 25,000,000 divided by 8,000, or 3,125 dollars, for A, and 25,000,000 divided by 7,200, about 3,472 dollars, for B. If both sell at 4,500 dollars per net square metre, A earns 36,000,000 dollars of revenue and B 32,400,000. Same cost, same price, and 3,600,000 dollars of difference from corridor and core layout alone. That is why the core position from Day 1 matters more than the lobby.

The same logic moves yield on cost for a rental building. Yield on cost is stabilised net operating income (NOI), the income left after operating expenses, divided by total project cost. More rentable area on the same cost lifts NOI and therefore yield on cost directly.

The premiums a ratio hides

Two more adjustments catch experienced people. The first is height. Taller buildings generally cost more per square metre, because they need larger structure and lateral systems, faster elevators, pressurised stairs, more pumping for water and longer crane hire, while each added floor brings only one floor of area. A benchmark from a building twice the height of yours, or half of it, needs a stated height adjustment from your cost consultant. The second is the parking. Structured or underground parking can carry a cost per square metre close to the building above it while producing no saleable area at all, so a benchmark that folds the garage into GFA looks cheap per square metre and expensive per unit. Ask for the garage separately, every time.

The test that ties all of this together is simple. When someone gives you a cost per square metre, repeat it back as a full sentence: hard cost, on gross area, at award date, in that city, at that finish, excluding these items. If they cannot complete the sentence, the number is a rumour.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

On your personal balance sheet, a development is recorded at what you can defend, not at what you hope. A budget built on an un-normalised benchmark overstates the equity you have created, because the true cost is higher than the budget says. When you estimate your own net worth, carry a project at cost until it is complete and valued, and keep a note of how much of your expected profit depends on a single benchmark number. If one number holds up a large share of your projected wealth, that is concentration in a form most people never notice. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any of this for your own affairs.

Professional sign-off required: quantity surveyor or cost consultant, on every benchmark adjustment used in a budget.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a budget built on a benchmark whose scope was narrower than yours, so that the missing items surface as change orders after the loan is sized. The control is a scope checklist attached to every benchmark, with each excluded item priced and added back before the number is used.

The beginner's mistake

Dividing total project cost by net saleable area for one building and hard cost by gross area for another, then comparing the two. Always state both definitions in the same sentence as the number.

Callback

In Week 13, Sage taught estimate classes: an early estimate deserves a wide range and a bought-out one a narrow range. A normalised benchmark is an early estimate, however precise it looks. Treat it as a range, carry contingency to match, and narrow it only as real quotes arrive.

Recap

A cost per square metre hides two definitions, cost and area. Normalise every benchmark for area basis, scope, date, location and quality before you use it. Efficiency, net over gross, turns the same construction cost into very different revenue, and it is visible in a finished building's core and corridors.

Next: Ivo on The Rules: what the code and the public record let you learn from a finished building, and what you may not take.
checklist: I ask what the cost includes and which area it is divided by before I use any benchmark.
I adjust every benchmark for date with a stated index.
I adjust for location and quality, and write each adjustment down.
I price and add back every item excluded from the benchmark's scope.
I calculate efficiency, net over gross, for every benchmark and every design option.
I carry a normalised benchmark as a range with matching contingency.
I have a cost consultant review every adjustment before it enters the budget.
head: Field checklist
speak: A cost per square metre hides two definitions: what counts as cost and which square metre. Cost may be hard cost only or the whole project including fees, finance and land. Area may be gross floor area, everything inside the outer walls, or net saleable area, what buyers pay for. To use a benchmark, normalise it on five points: area basis, scope, date, location and quality. In a hypothetical example, a headline of 2,400 dollars a square metre becomes about 2,480 once you add escalation, adjust for a dearer market and a richer finish, and add back excluded site works. Then look at efficiency, net area over gross. Two designs with identical cost and price can differ by millions in revenue purely because of core and corridor layout. Carry every benchmark as a range, and have a cost consultant check each adjustment.
terms: Gross floor area — the total area inside the outer walls on every floor, including corridors, shafts and plant rooms.
Net saleable area — the floor area a buyer actually purchases, excluding common areas and building services.
Efficiency ratio — net saleable or rentable area divided by gross floor area, showing how much of what you build you can sell or rent.

hostile.q: Your budget says 2,300 dollars a square metre. The tower you keep pointing to cost 2,400. Why should I believe you can build cheaper?
hostile.a: I am not claiming cheaper. The 2,400 was hard cost on gross area, three years old, in a dearer market with a richer finish and site works excluded. Normalised to our date, market, finish and scope, it is about 2,480 on the same basis our budget uses. Our 2,300 is a contractor's estimate that we have not yet bought out, so I carry it as a range of roughly 2,300 to 2,500 with contingency sized to the top of that range. If the bought-out number lands above it, the contingency absorbs it before the equity does.

title: What the Code and the Record Let You Take From a Finished Building
summary: A finished building can teach you its ideas, but not hand you its code compliance or its drawings. Ivo explains why a building permitted under an earlier code edition is not a template, how the public record works, and why copying drawings is a legal problem as well as a technical one.
body:
You may learn from any building you can see, but its code approval belongs to its own edition, its own occupancy and its own site, and its drawings belong to the people who made them.

Recall

Q. What is a recovery schedule?

A. A revised schedule, with named resources and logic, that shows how the contractor will regain lost time, usually required by the contract when progress falls behind.

Q. What is exposure class in concrete design?

A. A classification of the environment a concrete member will face, such as freezing and thawing, sulfates or chlorides, which sets limits on the mix and the cover to protect durability.

Q. What two definitions hide inside a cost per square metre?

A. What counts as cost, and which area is the divisor, gross floor area or net saleable area.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the most dangerous sentence in benchmarking is "they did it next door, so we can do it too." A finished building shows you what was approved for that building, under the code edition in force when its permit was issued, for its occupancy classification, on its site. Your building will be reviewed under the edition in force when you apply, with whatever local amendments apply then. The design may look identical. The answer may not be.

This lesson is about the line between learning and borrowing. You may learn from anything you can lawfully see: the shape of a floor plate, the position of a core, the sequence of trades. What you cannot borrow is the approval that made it legal, or the documents that describe it. Get that line right and benchmarking is the cheapest education in development. Get it wrong and it becomes the most expensive redesign of your project.

The code basis travels with the permit, not with the design

Plain English first. In the United States, most jurisdictions adopt a model code, usually the International Building Code (IBC), with local amendments, and update the adopted edition every few years. A building is judged against the edition adopted when its permit application was filed. Once built, it is generally allowed to stay as it is unless it changes use, is substantially altered or the authority finds an unsafe condition. That is why an older building can legally have features a new one may not.

The professional framing is the code basis: the occupancy classification, construction type, sprinkler status, allowable height and area, and fire-resistance ratings on which the approval rests. Each one interacts with the others. Change the occupancy from residential to transient, the way an apartment building becomes a hotel, and the requirements can change across the building. Week 100 covered that classification in depth.

Worked example one, hypothetical. You admire the corridor and stair layout of a residential tower permitted eight years ago. You copy it into a new design. Your code consultant finds that the current adopted edition, with a local amendment, now requires additional measures for the high-rise stairs and a different arrangement for one exit path. The layout that worked there needs redesign here. Nothing about the older building was wrong. It simply answered an older question. The rule is to treat any feature you copy as a proposal, and to run it through your own code analysis under the current adopted edition before it reaches your drawings. Verify any specific requirement against the current adopted edition and local amendments.

Say that out loud now.

A building's approval belongs to its own edition, occupancy and site. I copy ideas, then I prove them under my own code basis.

What the public record can tell you

Many building departments keep records that the public may request: the permit, its issue date, inspection sign-offs, the certificate of occupancy, sometimes the code analysis sheet on the permit drawings. Access rules differ by jurisdiction, and some records, especially detailed security or structural drawings, may be restricted. Where you can see them, the certificate of occupancy usually states the occupancy group, the construction type and the occupant load, which is a great deal of the code basis on one page.

Worked example two, hypothetical. A certificate of occupancy shows residential occupancy, a fully sprinklered building, and a construction type you would not have guessed from the street. The permit history shows a revision mid-construction. You now know three useful facts: the code path the designer chose, that the building relies on its sprinkler system for part of its allowances, and that something changed during construction. The third fact is a question for the builder, not an answer. Never treat a public record as complete; it shows what was filed, not why.

Accessibility, energy and the other codes in the building

The building code is not the only rulebook a finished building answers to, and the others change on their own cycles. Accessibility requirements in the United States come from the building code's accessibility provisions, which reference the ICC A117.1 standard, and from federal civil rights law, including the Fair Housing Act for many multifamily buildings and the Americans with Disabilities Act for public and commercial spaces. Energy requirements come from an adopted energy code, often the International Energy Conservation Code or ASHRAE 90.1. Fire protection systems follow NFPA standards adopted by reference. Each was in force at a particular edition when the benchmark was permitted. A facade that met an older energy code may fail the current one; a unit layout that was acceptable may not meet the current accessibility standard. Verify each against the current adopted edition before you rely on it.

So when you reverse engineer a building's design, keep a short table: the feature you want, the codes that govern it, the edition the benchmark was approved under, and the edition you will face. The table takes an hour. It is the cheapest insurance in design.

What you may not take

Drawings and specifications are generally protected by copyright, and standard design agreements in the United States, including widely used AIA forms, commonly treat them as the design professional's instruments of service, licensed to the owner for that project. That is commercial and contract practice backed by copyright law, not a building code rule; read the actual agreement. Using another owner's drawings to build your own project can expose you to a claim, even if you obtained them innocently. Ideas, dimensions you measure yourself and published information are a different matter, but the line is legal, not technical.

The same caution applies to benchmark data shared under a non-disclosure agreement (NDA), a contract restricting use and disclosure of confidential information. If a contractor shares another client's cost breakdown with you, ask whether he was entitled to. A contractor who shows you someone else's numbers will show someone else yours.

Professional sign-off required: registered architect or code consultant, on the code basis of any feature you adopt; lawyer, on the use of any drawings or confidential data from another project.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a design that inherits a code approval it does not have, discovered at plan review or, worse, at inspection, after the structure has been built around it. The control is a code analysis for your own building under the current adopted edition, prepared before schematic design is frozen, with every copied feature listed and checked.

The beginner's mistake

Asking a friendly contractor for "the drawings from the last one" to save design fees. It saves nothing. It imports a code basis that may not apply, a set of site assumptions that are not yours and a possible copyright claim.

Callback

In Week 82, Vera taught that records are evidence and that a record shows what was filed, not what was meant. The public file on a finished building is exactly that kind of record. Read it for dates, classifications and revisions, then go and ask why.

Recap

A finished building's approval rests on its own code edition, occupancy, construction type and site. Copy ideas, then prove them under your own code basis. Use the public record for dates and classifications, never as a complete story. Drawings and confidential data from other projects belong to others.

Next: Quincy on The Numbers: working backward from a finished building's dates and price to its cost and floor cycle.
checklist: I treat every feature copied from another building as a proposal to be checked.
I confirm the current adopted code edition and local amendments for my site before design.
I prepare my own code analysis before schematic design is frozen.
I request the public permit file and certificate of occupancy where the law allows it.
I read public records for dates, classifications and revisions, then ask why.
I never use another project's drawings without written legal clearance.
I ask whether anyone sharing another client's data was entitled to share it.
I get an architect or code consultant to sign off the code basis.
head: Field checklist
speak: A finished building can teach you ideas, but its code approval belongs to its own code edition, occupancy, construction type and site. In the United States most places adopt the International Building Code with local amendments, update it every few years, and judge a building against the edition in force when its permit was filed. So a layout that was compliant eight years ago may need redesign today. Treat every copied feature as a proposal, and prove it in your own code analysis under the current adopted edition before design is frozen. The public record, where you may see it, often shows the permit dates, the certificate of occupancy, the occupancy group and the construction type. It shows what was filed, not why. And drawings are generally protected as the designer's instruments of service; using another project's drawings is a legal problem, not a shortcut.
terms: Code basis — the occupancy classification, construction type, sprinkler status, height and area and ratings on which a building's approval rests.
Certificate of occupancy — the document issued by the building authority allowing a building or part of it to be occupied for a stated use.
Instruments of service — the drawings, specifications and other documents a design professional produces, commonly owned by the designer and licensed to the owner for one project.

hostile.q: Your architect copied the stair core from the tower across the road. It passed there. Why are you paying for a new code review?
hostile.a: Because that tower was approved under the edition in force when its permit was filed, for its own occupancy and site. We will be reviewed under the edition adopted when we apply, with the local amendments in force then. Our code consultant has checked the copied core against the current edition and listed two changes. Paying for that review now costs a few weeks of design time. Discovering the same two changes at plan review would cost a redesign of the core and every floor around it.

title: Working Backward From a Finished Building to Its Cycle and Its Cost
summary: Starting from what a finished building publicly shows, its dates, its area and its sale price, Quincy works backward step by step to its average floor cycle and its likely hard cost per square metre. The lesson is the method and the range, not a single answer.
body:
You can reverse engineer a finished building's floor cycle from its permit and occupancy dates, and its hard cost from its sale price, but only as a range, and only if you write down every assumption you add along the way.

Recall

Q. How do you estimate floor-to-floor height from the street?

A. Estimate the total height, subtract an allowance for the ground floor and the roof structure, and divide what remains by the number of typical floors.

Q. What is the difference between excusable and compensable delay?

A. Excusable delay entitles the contractor to more time. Compensable delay entitles it to time and money. Which events fall where is set by the contract.

Q. Why are concrete cylinders usually tested at more than one age?

A. Early tests show how strength is developing and warn of trouble; the test at the age the specification names, often 28 days, shows whether the concrete met the specified strength.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is an even-numbered week, so we start from a finished outcome and work backward. The outcome is a hypothetical building completed and sold in your market. The questions are the ones you will ask before your own project: how fast did they really build, and what did it really cost? Brokers will give you a headline. Working backward gives you a defensible range and, more valuable still, the list of facts you need to narrow it.

The facts we start from

All figures are hypothetical. A residential building has 20 typical floors of 800 square metres of gross floor area each, above a 2-level podium of 1,600 square metres per level. Total gross floor area is 20 times 800, which is 16,000 square metres, plus 2 times 1,600, which is 3,200, for 19,200 square metres. Public records show a building permit in month 0 and an occupancy certificate in month 22. A land transfer record shows the developer paid 8,000,000 dollars for the site. A press report says the completed building was sold for 80,000,000 dollars.

Step by step: the floor cycle

Step 1, convert months to working days. Use 21 working days a month, a common planning assumption. 22 months times 21 gives 462 working days from permit to occupancy.

Step 2, remove the work that is not typical floors. Assume 4 months, 84 working days, for excavation, foundations and below-grade work. Assume 2 months, 42 working days, for the 2 podium levels. Assume 6 months, 126 working days, for the work that follows top-out: the last facade, fit-out of the upper floors, commissioning and inspections. Total removed: 84 plus 42 plus 126, which is 252 working days.

Step 3, what remains is the typical-floor window. 462 less 252 gives 210 working days.

Step 4, divide by the floors. 210 working days over 20 floors gives an average of 10.5 working days per floor.

Step 5, compare with the best floor. Suppose the builder tells you, on the tour, that the best typical floor was done in 7 working days. The gap between 7 and 10.5 is 3.5 working days per floor, or 3.5 times 20, which is 70 working days. That is the time lost to weather, crane breakdown, inspections, concrete supply and the learning curve on the first floors. The best floor is what the system could do. The average is what the project did.

Say that out loud now.

The best floor is what the system could do. The average is what the project did. I plan on the average.

Step by step: the hard cost

Now work backward from the price. We need three assumptions, each labelled.

Step 1, assume a developer's margin. Margin on cost is commercial practice, not a standard, and it varies with market and risk. Assume the developer earned 15 percent on total development cost. Then total development cost equals 80,000,000 divided by 1.15, which is about 69,600,000 dollars.

Step 2, remove the land. 69,600,000 less 8,000,000 gives about 61,600,000 dollars for everything except land.

Step 3, split hard costs from soft and finance costs. Assume soft costs, design, permits and fees, plus finance costs, interest and loan fees, together equal 25 percent of hard cost. Then hard cost times 1.25 equals 61,600,000, so hard cost is 61,600,000 divided by 1.25, about 49,300,000 dollars.

Step 4, divide by area. 49,300,000 dollars divided by 19,200 square metres gives about 2,570 dollars per square metre of gross floor area.

Testing the range

A single answer here would be false precision, so change one assumption at a time. If the margin was 20 percent rather than 15, total development cost is 80,000,000 divided by 1.20, about 66,700,000; less land, 58,700,000; divided by 1.25, about 46,900,000; divided by 19,200, about 2,440 dollars per square metre. If the margin stays at 15 percent but soft and finance costs were 30 percent of hard cost, hard cost is 61,600,000 divided by 1.30, about 47,400,000, or about 2,470 dollars per square metre.

So the defensible statement is: hard cost was probably between about 2,440 and 2,570 dollars per square metre of gross floor area, if the sale price, the land price and our three assumptions hold. Then list what would narrow it: the actual margin, the actual finance cost, which depends on the loan and the duration we have just estimated, and whether the sale price included furniture or a parking structure.

Notice how the two calculations connect. The 22-month duration we derived drives the finance cost, because interest runs for the whole build. A slower build means more interest, a larger soft and finance share and therefore a lower implied hard cost for the same sale price. Reverse engineering is one model, not two separate sums.

A third check: crane months

A reverse-engineered schedule can be checked against equipment, because equipment is expensive and visible in photographs. Suppose site photographs in the public press show one tower crane from the start of the podium to top-out. The podium took 42 working days and the typical floors 210, so the crane worked about 252 working days, or 252 divided by 21, which is 12 months, plus erection and dismantling, call it 13 crane-months. At a hypothetical all-in cost of 40,000 dollars a crane-month, including operator and maintenance, that is about 520,000 dollars. Now test the cycle: if the builder had planned a 7-day average with the same single crane, the typical floors would have taken 140 working days, and with the podium 182 working days, so the crane about 8.7 months plus erection and dismantling, under 10 months. A builder who could save about 3 crane-months and 70 working days of interest by adding a second hoist, as tomorrow's tour will suggest, had a cheap trade available. That is the kind of conclusion reverse engineering exists to produce.

Professional sign-off required: quantity surveyor or cost consultant, before any reverse-engineered cost is used in a budget or shown to a lender.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is reporting the midpoint as if it were a measurement. A reverse-engineered number built on three assumptions can be wrong by more than your contingency. The control is to present it always as a range, with the assumptions printed beside it, and to replace each assumption with a verified fact before it drives a decision.

The beginner's mistake

Planning your own schedule on the builder's best floor. The best floor is a capability; the average is a forecast. Plan on the average, and treat any gain on it as float you earned.

Callback

In Week 44, Roman taught stress tests: base, downside and severe cases, and the break-even that shows how far an assumption can move before the deal fails. Today's range is the same idea run backward. Every assumption you add to a reverse-engineered number is a variable; test each one, see which moves the answer most, and that is the fact you go and verify first.

Recap

From dates, area, land price and sale price we derived an average floor cycle of about 10.5 working days against a best floor of 7, and a hard cost range of roughly 2,440 to 2,570 dollars per square metre. Every figure rests on labelled assumptions. Present ranges, connect duration to finance cost, and plan on the average floor.

Next: Marco on The Room: the benchmark tour, and how to get the truth from the contractor who built it.
checklist: I start every reverse calculation from verified public facts and label each one.
I convert months to working days with a stated assumption.
I remove non-typical work before I divide by floors.
I compare the average floor cycle with the best floor and plan on the average.
I label every margin, soft-cost and finance assumption as commercial practice.
I change one assumption at a time and report a range, never a midpoint.
I connect the derived duration to the finance cost.
I list the facts that would narrow the range and go and verify the most sensitive one.
head: Field checklist
speak: Working backward from a hypothetical finished building of 19,200 square metres, permitted in month 0 and occupied in month 22, gives 462 working days. Remove 84 for foundations, 42 for the podium and 126 for work after top-out, and 210 working days remain for 20 typical floors, an average of 10.5 days a floor. If the best floor took 7, the project lost 70 working days to weather, breakdowns, inspections and the learning curve. Plan on the average. For cost, start from an 80,000,000 dollar sale, assume a 15 percent margin, remove 8,000,000 of land and assume soft and finance costs at 25 percent of hard cost. That implies about 2,570 dollars a square metre. Change one assumption at a time and the range runs from about 2,440 to 2,570. Present the range, print the assumptions, and verify the most sensitive one first.
terms: Working day — a planning unit counting only days on which site work normally proceeds, excluding weekends and holidays.
Margin on cost — a developer's profit expressed as a percentage of total development cost; a commercial measure, not a standard.
Soft costs — project costs other than construction and land, such as design, permits, legal, marketing and fees.

hostile.q: You say the tower down the road cost about 2,500 a square metre. Where did that number come from?
hostile.a: It is a range, roughly 2,440 to 2,570, not a single number. I worked back from the public sale price and land price, with three assumptions I can show you: the developer's margin, the soft and finance share, and that the price excluded furniture and parking. The sensitivity is on the page; margin moves it most. I have not used it in our budget. Our budget uses our cost consultant's estimate, and this range is a cross-check that tells us whether that estimate is plausible.

title: The Benchmark Tour: Getting the Truth From the Builder
summary: A scene on a tour of a recently completed hypothetical tower with the builder's project director. Marco shows which questions get real answers, which lines close the conversation, what the questions behind the questions are, and how to leave with facts rather than a sales pitch.
body:
On a benchmark tour the builder will show you the best floor and tell you the best story; your job is to get the average, the trouble and the one thing they would do differently, without asking for anything they cannot give.

Recall

Q. In Ford's composite, what was the point of no return?

A. The first day the slab formwork was stripped at 3 days without a measured in-place strength. After that the job was carrying fresh slabs on unproven concrete.

Q. When a contractor's notice of delay arrives late, what is your first move?

A. Acknowledge receipt in writing without waiving any contractual right, log the date, and send the notice and the contract clause to your adviser before you discuss entitlement.

Q. What is a mix design?

A. The specified proportions of cement, other cementitious materials, water, aggregates and admixtures for a concrete, chosen to meet strength, durability and workability requirements.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a tour of a finished building is one of the few times a competitor's or a contractor's real experience is available to you for the price of a morning. It is also a sales meeting. The project director wants your next job, or wants his firm to look good. Both are fine. You simply need to know which part of what you hear is evidence and which part is marketing.

The scene

A hypothetical 20-floor residential tower finished last year. You are with its builder's project director on a typical floor, then on the roof, then in the basement plant room. You arranged the visit through the building's owner, who agreed to a two-hour walk and nothing more. You have five questions written on one card in your pocket.

Lines to say

"What did your typical floor cycle average across the whole building, not your best floor?" The average is the number you will plan on.

"Which floor was hardest, and why?" This invites a story about trouble, which is where the lessons are.

"What would you change if you built it again tomorrow?" Most builders have an answer ready, and it is usually the most valuable sentence of the day.

"How many cranes and hoists did you run, and when did each one come down?" Equipment is the system behind the cycle.

"Who on the owner's side made decisions, and how quickly did you get answers?" This tells you how much of the schedule depended on the owner, which means on you next time.

Say that out loud now.

What did your cycle average, which floor was hardest, and what would you change tomorrow?

Lines never to say

"Can you send me your drawings?" Ivo explained on Day 4 why that is not his to give. Asking for it also tells him you might misuse other people's information.

"We'll beat your schedule." It invites him to stop teaching you and start defending himself.

"What did the owner pay you?" It is confidential, and a builder who answers it will answer it about you.

"That's amazing." Admiration is fine; a running commentary of it turns a fact-finding visit into a compliment exchange, and you will leave with nothing written down.

The question behind the question

When he says, "We topped out two months early," the question behind it is: early against what? Against the contract date, which may have carried float? Against a revised baseline? Ask, gently: "Early against the original baseline or the revised one?" When he says, "No real problems with the facade," the question behind it is whether the facade was tested. Ask: "Did you run field water tests, and how many failed the first time?" A good builder respects that question; it is exactly what a good owner asks.

When you ask about the owner's decisions and he pauses before answering, that pause is data. It usually means approvals were slow and he is deciding whether to criticise the person who arranged your visit. Do not press. Note it, and say: "That's helpful. Owners are often the bottleneck, and I'd rather know it in advance."

When to stay silent

After you ask what he would change, stop talking. Count to five if you must. People fill silence with their most honest second thought. The first answer is often polished; the one that follows the pause is often the real one.

Stay silent, too, in the plant room. Let him explain the systems in his own order. The order a builder chooses tells you what he thinks mattered and what caused him trouble.

Holding your state

You may feel that you are the least experienced person on the floor. You probably are, and that is the purpose of the visit. Keep your questions short and your voice level. Write numbers down in front of him; it signals that you take them seriously and it slows the conversation to a pace where accuracy improves. If he is condescending, do not compete. Ask the next question. Composure in a room you do not own is a skill, and benchmark tours are a safe place to practise it.

A worked example: turning the tour into numbers

Hypothetical. He tells you: best floor 7 working days, average about 10, one crane until month 16, one external hoist added at floor 8, facade 4 floors behind the slab, and that he would add a second hoist earlier next time. Within an hour of leaving, you write: implied 3 lost days per floor over 20 floors, 60 working days, largely from vertical transport; hoist added late; facade lag of 4 floors. Your own schedule now carries an average cycle of 10, a hoist from the first typical floor priced at a stated monthly rate, and a facade lag target. One tour has given you three concrete schedule decisions.

A second example, hypothetical. He says field water tests on the windows failed on 3 of the first 10 locations, then passed after a sealant change. You add a mock-up and early field testing to your quality plan, and ask your envelope consultant to specify the test method and the pass criteria before award.

If the owner joins the tour

Sometimes the building's owner walks with you, and the conversation changes. The builder becomes more careful, because his client is listening, and the owner becomes the better source on two subjects: what the building costs to run and what the buyers or tenants complained about after moving in. Ask the owner: "What was the first complaint after occupancy?" and "Which system costs you more to run than you expected?" Those two answers tell you about the decisions that only show up after the builder has gone home, which is the part of a building's life your own project will live longest.

Do not ask the owner about the builder's performance in front of the builder. If the answer matters, ask for ten minutes alone at the end, or a call the following week. And whatever you learn, thank both of them in writing the same day, naming one specific thing you learned. People who are thanked precisely agree to the next visit.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is leaving with the builder's best story instead of his average experience, and planning on it. The control is the card in your pocket: five questions that ask for averages, trouble and changes, answered in writing before you leave.

The beginner's mistake

Spending the tour in the show suite. The lessons are in the riser rooms, on the roof and in the basement, where the systems, the equipment and the compromises live.

Callback

In Week 5, Kema taught that listening is a skill with structure: ask, pause, reflect back and then ask again. A benchmark tour is that skill applied to a technical subject, and the pause after "what would you change?" is where the structure earns its keep.

Recap

Ask for averages, the hardest floor and what he would change. Never ask for drawings, prices or praise. Hear the question behind "early" and "no problems". Stay silent after the hard question, write numbers down, and turn the tour into schedule and quality decisions within the hour.

Next: Kema on Quiz and Recap, with Cole's Auditor's Chair on a benchmarking memo.
checklist: I arrange benchmark visits through the owner and agree the scope of the visit.
I bring five written questions that ask for averages, trouble and changes.
I ask for the average floor cycle, not the best floor.
I ask what the builder would change and stay silent after asking.
I never ask for drawings, contract prices or another owner's confidential data.
I spend most of the tour in plant rooms, risers and on the roof.
I write down numbers in front of the builder.
Within an hour I turn what I heard into schedule and quality decisions.
head: Field checklist
speak: On a benchmark tour, the builder shows his best floor and tells his best story. Your job is to get the average, the trouble and what he would change. Ask: what did the typical floor cycle average, not the best floor; which floor was hardest and why; what would you change tomorrow; how many cranes and hoists, and when did each come down; and how quickly did the owner decide. Never ask for drawings, prices or another owner's confidential data, and do not promise to beat his schedule. Listen for the question behind the question: early against which baseline, no problems on the facade according to which tests. After the hard question, stay silent; the honest answer often comes second. Spend the time in the plant rooms and on the roof, write numbers down in front of him, and convert what you heard into schedule decisions within the hour.
terms: Benchmark tour — a visit to a completed building to learn how it was designed and built, usually arranged with its owner and builder.
Baseline schedule — the approved original schedule against which progress, delay and float are measured.
Field water test — an on-site test spraying water at windows or facade joints under set conditions to check for leaks.

hostile.q: You toured our competitor's building with their builder. Did you take anything you should not have?
hostile.a: No. The visit was arranged with the building's owner, limited to a two-hour walk, and I asked only about the builder's own experience: average cycle, equipment, sequence and what he would change. I did not ask for or receive drawings, prices or the owner's data, and my notes record only what was said and what I could see. I can show you those notes. What we took away were three scheduling decisions and a test requirement, which are ideas, not anyone's documents.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 120 Review: Reading a Building Backwards
summary: Kema reviews the week on reverse engineering a finished building: the four passes, the borrowed floor cycle and Rule 120, normalising cost per square metre, code basis, working backward to cycle and cost, and the benchmark tour. Cole's Auditor's Chair reads a benchmarking memo as a hostile auditor would.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: a finished building is evidence, and you learn from it by reconstructing the system that produced it, never by borrowing its headline numbers.

Recall

Q. What is efficiency in a floor plate?

A. Net saleable or rentable area divided by gross floor area. Two buildings with the same cost and price can earn very different revenue because of core and corridor layout.

Q. What is a time bar, in one sentence?

A. A clause that makes timely notice a condition of a claim, so that late notice can defeat an otherwise valid entitlement, subject to the wording and the governing law.

Q. Why is adding water to a concrete truck on site controlled?

A. Because it raises the water-cement ratio, which lowers strength and durability, so any addition must stay within what the approved mix design allows.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the buildings in your market are a library you can read for free. If you can answer these six questions without notes, you can walk through any completed tower and come out with decisions instead of impressions. Answer each one aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. Name the four passes for reading a finished building.

Answer: Structure, systems, sequence and cost, in that order, because each one constrains the next.

Question 2. Why is a floor cycle an output, not a target?

Answer: Because it is produced by a system: cranes, hoists, formwork, reinforcement method, concrete mix, crew experience and inspection flow. Copy the number without the system and you have copied a promise you cannot keep.

Question 3. State Rule 120.

Answer: Never adopt a benchmark cycle time until its crane, formwork, labour, concrete and inspection system is matched, and never strip or reshore on the calendar; strip only on in-place strength the engineer of record has approved.

Question 4. What five points must you normalise before using a benchmark cost per square metre?

Answer: Area basis, scope, date, location and quality, plus any height or parking adjustment, each written down.

Question 5. Why can a feature that was compliant on an older building fail on yours?

Answer: Because a building is judged against the code edition, local amendments, occupancy and site that applied when its permit was filed. Yours will be judged against the edition in force when you apply.

Question 6. On a benchmark tour, which number do you plan on, and why?

Answer: The average floor cycle, not the best floor. The best floor shows what the system could do; the average shows what the project did, including weather, breakdowns and inspections.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Ford and Marco taught the four passes and the early decisions that drive a building: grid, core, floor-to-floor and repetition. Ford took a composite case in which a borrowed 4-day cycle met a one-crane site and early stripping cracked a slab, giving Rule 120. Quincy normalised a benchmark cost and showed how efficiency moves revenue. Ivo explained why a code approval belongs to its own edition and why drawings belong to their authors. Quincy worked backward from dates and a sale price to an average cycle and a cost range. Marco ran the benchmark tour.

Cole's Auditor's Chair

Week 120 is a fourth week, so the Red Pen becomes Cole's Auditor's Chair: read this hypothetical benchmarking memo as a hostile auditor would. Find the defects before reading on.

Memo to the Investment Committee. Benchmark: Tower B, a comparable residential building. Tower B was built for 2,300 dollars per square metre in 18 months with a 5-day cycle. Our project is similar in size, so we have adopted 2,300 dollars per square metre and an 18-month programme in the base case, which reduces contingency to 3 percent. Source: conversation with the Tower B builder's project director. Prepared by the development manager.

The defects. First, the cost has no area basis: gross or net, and the memo does not say. Second, it has no scope: hard cost only, or including site works, parking and fees. Third, it has no date or location adjustment, so a figure from another year or market is used as if it were today's. Fourth, the 5-day cycle is almost certainly a best floor from a conversation, not an average, and the memo does not say which crane, formwork or mix produced it. Fifth, "similar in size" is not a test of comparability; height, efficiency and finish matter more than size. Sixth, contingency has been cut because of a benchmark, which inverts the logic: an unverified benchmark should widen the range, not narrow it. Seventh, the only source is a sales conversation, with no document, no public record and no cost consultant review.

Then the auditor asks for the evidence behind each claim, and that list is the real lesson. For the cost: the area basis, the scope schedule, the base date and the index used to update it. For the duration: the permit and occupancy dates from the public record. For the cycle: the average across all typical floors and the equipment that produced it. For contingency: the estimate class of the current budget and the reasoning for the percentage. For the source: who reviewed it independently. A benchmark that cannot produce its evidence is a story, and a story is not a basis for cutting contingency.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to a partner who asks, "Why are we spending time studying other people's buildings?" Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "Because every finished building in our market is a record of decisions someone else paid for. We read it in four passes: how it stands up, how its systems work, how it was sequenced and what it cost per useful square metre. That shows us the early choices that drove everything, the grid, the core, the floor height and how much repeats. We use public permit and occupancy dates to estimate how fast it was really built, and we normalise any cost we hear for area, scope, date, location and quality. We never borrow a cycle time or a cost without the system that produced it; that is how a famous four-day cycle becomes a cracked slab. And we copy ideas, never drawings, because a code approval belongs to its own edition and a drawing belongs to its author. The result is a schedule and budget built on ranges we can defend."

Score your own answer before comparing. Did you open with the bottom line? Did you name the four passes? Did you say that a benchmark is the output of a system? Did you finish inside two minutes? If you missed any, record it again tomorrow.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is false confidence from a benchmark: a number heard from a credible person, used without its conditions, that narrows your contingency at the moment you know least. The control is a benchmark file with a source, a basis and a conditions list for every number, reviewed by a cost consultant.

The beginner's mistake

Treating the most impressive building as the best benchmark. The best benchmark is the most comparable one, with the most verifiable facts, even if it is plain.

Callback

In Week 2, you learned the outside view: before trusting your own forecast, look at how similar projects actually turned out. Reverse engineering finished buildings is the outside view made physical. Each building you read is one more member of your reference class, and the average of a reference class is a better forecast than the best story inside it.

Recap

Read buildings in four passes, copy systems rather than numbers, normalise every cost, prove copied features under your own code basis, work backward to ranges, and get averages on the tour. Rule 120 keeps the formwork on until the concrete has earned its removal.

head: The six questions
speak: This week we learned to read a finished building backwards. Four passes: structure, systems, sequence and cost. Find the early decisions that drove everything: the grid, the core position, the floor-to-floor height and how much of the design repeats. Treat every benchmark number as the output of a system. A borrowed four-day cycle on a one-crane site, recovered by stripping formwork on the calendar, cracked a slab and turned six weeks into five months; Rule 120 says strip only on in-place strength the engineer of record has approved. Normalise any cost per square metre for area basis, scope, date, location and quality. Prove any copied feature under your own code edition, and never use another project's drawings. Work backward from public dates and prices to ranges, not midpoints. On a tour, ask for the average floor, the hardest floor and what the builder would change.
terms: Benchmark — a completed comparable project used as a reference point for cost, schedule or design, valid only with its conditions stated.
Reference class — a group of similar past projects whose actual outcomes form the outside view for a new forecast.
Normalisation — adjusting a benchmark number for area basis, scope, date, location and quality so it can be compared with your own.

hostile.q: Your investment committee memo cut contingency to 3 percent on the strength of a benchmark. Defend it.
hostile.a: I cannot, and I have withdrawn it. The benchmark cost had no stated area basis, scope, date or location, the cycle time came from a conversation and was almost certainly a best floor, and the only source was the builder's project director. An unverified benchmark should widen our range, not narrow it. The revised memo carries the benchmark as a cross-check range, keeps contingency at the level our estimate class supports, and lists the four facts we are verifying before any further change.
